    #89553. Hybrid won the in-housing debate, at least among the largest advertisers

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1267 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Hybrid won the in-housing debate, at least among the largest advertisers

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Recent findings suggest that reports of the media agency’s death remain greatly exaggerated.
    • Advertisers are carving up the media operation with more intent, keeping the work that sits closest to the brand and handing the sprawling specialist stuff back to their agencies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Recent findings suggest that reports of the media agency’s death remain greatly exaggerated. Its job description, however, is another story.

    Advertisers are carving up the media operation with more intent, keeping the work that sits closest to the brand and handing the sprawling specialist stuff back to their agencies.

    The shift has been playing out in fits and starts for the best part of a decade. COMvergence’s first Global Advertiser Survey shows how far its got. The media agency research firm polled 28 senior marketing, media, procurement and operations leaders at 21 global advertisers, who between them control more than $22 billion in media spend. A quarter of them buy or control media in-house. Of the rest, around a third are thinking about bringing spend in-house over the next 12 months.

    “It’s a bit like a football club,” said Jon Williams, founder and chief creative officer at Freedom Works, a collective of senior agency execs who help brands build in-house teams. “You build your own academy and you’re proud of it. You still buy a striker when you need goals. You just don’t keep a dozen agents on the payroll in case.”.

    Whether they’ve started in-housing or are still weighing it up, few advertisers want to take everything off their agency’s plate. Most would rather divide the work. Nearly 80% of respondents described their setup as hybrid, mixing internal teams with agency support. Fewer than 18% run media entirely in-house.

    “The CMO isn’t always the one pushing,” stated Scott Grenz, head of U.S. operations for COMvergence. “Much of the energy comes from internal media, procurement and data/analytics teams. They believe owning their data and getting full transparency are key to media effectiveness, and that often leads to bringing parts of the digital media scope in-house.

    “Agencies have become more transparent, and advertisers are looking at their media ecosystem as a whole, asking how best to use all their resources, internal and external, to hit their critical KPIs, said Grenz.

    It has been revealed that which is to say the motive for in-housing has moved from saving money to getting better at specific things. Mars is staffing internal teams to get ready for agentic shopping, while Gap has gone as far as setting up its own entertainment studio. Lego brought programmatic in-house partly so it could make better informed calls on which ad tech vendors to use. Its agency, and its vendors, can expect sharper questions as a result.

    “When I started out, the in-house studio was where ads went to get resized,” said Williams. “The agency did the thinking and the studio did the cutdowns. Nobody would say that now.”.

    Recent findings suggest that getting here took the best part of a decade. For most of that time, in-housing was a cost and transparency play with advertisers chasing cheaper media and a clearer view of where the money went. The ANA’s 2016 report on agency rebates gave plenty of them reason to look. Somewhere along the way, the question moved on to what their own teams could do faster or better.

    In-house teams tend to go where the budgets are, which for most advertisers means digital. The largest group of respondents put 60% to 70% of total media spend into digital and plenty go higher, according to the report. Only a very small minority keep digital below 30%.

    Unsurprisingly, social media is where advertisers are most willing to take the wheel. More than 85% of the in house operators in the survey run social themselves. Search display and programmatic trail at roughly 57%. The logic is simple enough. Social rewards fast decisions and direct access to audience data, both of which come easier when the team sits inside the business.

    Industry observers note that the same can’t be stated of retail media, CTV and influencer marketing. They remain mostly agency-run, with relatively few advertisers taking them on directly. All three are fragmented and specialized enough to keep agencies in demand. Take Retail media. Its sprawl of networks and measurement approaches is the sort of mess advertisers seem happy to pay someone else to untangle. Several respondents still named influencer, commerce and retail media as where they’re experimenting with newly introduced models or looking for outside guidance.

    Recent findings suggest that “Building an in-house media practice is hard. It carries real risk, takes significant resources and requires capabilities many advertisers don’t have yet,” mentioned Grenz.” Still, there are plenty of use cases across the industry, from massive advertisers and small, and no single model has won out. Our data shows that many advertisers who have in-housed still work with a media agency. That’s the real takeaway: it isn’t all or nothing. Advertisers are working out the right mix of internal and external expertise to make their media effective.”.

    According to recent reports, for all the talk of brands doing more on their own, agency rosters remain crowded. More than half (54) of the marketers COMvergence interviewed use more than one media agency and more than half bring in digital specialist agencies alongside their main one.

    In a recent development, still, that crowding probably won’t last. More than 80% of the advertisers working with multiple agencies strategy to simplify or consolidate. They want specialist expertise and fewer partners at the same time — a tension that should keep the pitch consultants busy for a while.

    “Some of it is procurement,” noted Williams. “One in-house lead told us it took nine months to get a upcoming supplier set up. Do that ten times and you’ll consolidate too. And AI is taking away a lot of the everyday work that used to keep four or five agencies busy.”.

    Half of the respondents use global hubs, offshore resources or both. Their comments pointed to India, Colombia, Brazil, Mexico and other regional centers, mostly handling digital operations, programmatic buying, social execution and support work.

    Advertisers see these setups as agency-run rather than as their own teams. That’s a handy calling card for holdcos selling scale. In fact, COMvergence expects hubs and offshore talent to become an even bigger differentiator for agencies as labor costs rise and more execution gets automated.

    “There’s no universal ceiling,” said Grenz. “It comes down to how each advertiser weighs the risk and reward of in-housing against agency management. Agencies have made a strong case that they’re a critical partner, and they’ve shown they’re willing to work within whatever hybrid model a client wants.”.

    It has been revealed that asked what they’d like more of, respondents pointed squarely at agency operating models, which made up more than 40% of all feedback. They want to see how peers structure internal teams, split work between brand and agency, govern media investment and run in-house functions.

    It has been revealed that the usual caveats apply to a report like this. Twenty one advertisers is a small sample so a handful of companies can swing a percentage by a lot. COMvergence looks to run the survey every year and the second edition should say more about the direction of travel than this first snapshot can.

    Even so, the findings are a good encapsulation of how senior marketers at the largest advertisers see where things are headed.

    Meta’s reported CTV expansion and AppLovin’s alleged interest in Criteo are foreboding for independent ad tech as major platforms extend their reach.

    HUMAN Security’s latest investigation queries the effectiveness of CTV verification safeguards.

    Advertisers continue to increase investments on the retail weekend but AI, tariffs and discounting pressure present banana skins.

    Brands boost Black Friday CTV, retail and search spending

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Industry observers note that brands are expected to spend 10-30% more on digital media activity over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, compared with 2025, according to five media buyers who spoke with Digiday.
    • Spending growth around Black Friday (Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Industry observers note that brands are expected to spend 10-30% more on digital media activity over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, compared with 2025, according to five media buyers who spoke with Digiday. Retail media, particularly Amazon, search, CTV and YouTube, are expected to soak up much of that increase.

    Spending growth around Black Friday (Nov. 27) and Cyber Monday (Nov. 30), the twin peaks of the holiday season for many retailers, hardly comes as a surprise. According to Triple Whale, 33,000 U.S. brands spent $607 million across the Black Friday/Cyber Monday period last year; this year, Bain Capital estimates U.S. companies to record $85 billion in sales over the five day period, accounting for 8.5% of total holiday spending for 2026.

    But there’s nuance to be considered, especially with retailers choosing to discount earlier in the year.

    “We expect higher spend across direct-response channels this year, though it varies by category and brand,” remarked Brett Fischer, associate director of performance media at e-commerce-focused media agency Collective Measures.

    For one, product discounting and marketing activity kicked off earlier this year. According to commerce media company Fluent, 32% of shoppers had already begun holiday purchases prior to Black Friday.

    Meanwhile, the number of products listed at a discount between Oct. 1-20 rose 56%, and increased 71% during the week preceding Prime Significant Deal Days, according to data from e-commerce company Wayvia. In 2025, the same discounting surge didn’t kick in until the middle of November.

    That’s driven budget increases, or forced some marketers to spread their ad dollars over a longer period of time. Nola Ladd, associate director of brand media at Collective Measures, said the agency’s clients had spread their ad dollars thinner over a longer period, with the aim of improving consumer consideration.

    “Mid-funnel investment is running roughly flat year over year,” mentioned Ladd. “Instead of growing it in this period, we’ve spread it across more of the year so brands are building consideration well before peak season.”.

    U.S. retail sales are expected to rise 4.2% this year compared with 2025, according to Oxford Economics, while the National Retail Federation (NRF) estimated that 182.7 million Americans will shop during the five-day run of discounts and sales, a slight reduction from 2025’s 186.9 million.

    In a recent development, for some retailers, heavy discounting in the run-up to Black Friday is beginning to bite. Data from media agency PMG found that weekly sales rose 10% during October’s Prime Substantial Deal Days (staged by Amazon on Oct. 6-7), with grocery purchases increasing 37.7% in volume. But the average selling price in that category fell 13.1%, while electronics revenues were “flat.”.

    “Many of our clients in CPG and home delivery are watching sell-through closely,” mentioned Scott Shamberg, president and CEO at media agency Mile Marker.

    “Many of our clients saw softness for the last few weeks but are still expecting to see demand and sales pick up,” noted Michelle Merklin, vp of search innovation and growth, Tinuiti.

    Companies affected by tariff-related cost increases will have to choose between crucial profit margin or the need to match competitors’ discounts. “It’s vital for brands to continue to stay competitive within this time frame,” said Carly Carson, head of integrated media at PMG.

    According to recent reports, “Our clients’ spend this Black Friday and Cyber Monday is mixed — some are flat and some are up. There has been some softening in the market the last quarter, so some clients are being conservative,” stated Josy Amann, co-founder, Ars X Machina (AXM).

    Per PMG data, brands that discounted across a larger range of their portfolio enjoyed a lot more growth during October: on average, those with 75% of their product set on discount saw 16% overall revenue growth, while companies that discounted 25% or less of their products saw overall revenues fall 11%.

    Sales softness, and increased cost of sales hasn’t led to clients risking a retreat from Black Friday spending — the weekend window is too vital a sales event for retailers. “We have definitely been making strong recommendations around maintaining a full-funnel strategy… BFCM is a great time to find fresh consumers in a shopping mindset,” said Amann.

    But some advertisers were shifting dollars into channels considered to be safer bets. “Less brand, more performance channels,” Shamberg explained. Merklin also said Tinuiti clients were, on the whole, choosing not to cut media budgets.

    Those safer bets include CTV and YouTube, as well as retail media options. According to Brock Berry, CEO of digital ad trafficking platform AdCellerant, the quantity of advertisers running CTV activity during November was 25% than the same period last year, despite CPMs running as much as 18% higher in some regions following high competition from political spenders during the midterm elections. Shamberg said he expected to see “double-digit growth” in each of those channels among Mile Marker clients.

    In a recent development, at the same time, product discovery behaviors are under question. A survey of 29,000 consumers commissioned by delivery firm DHL estimated that 90% of shoppers used generative AI chatbots or assistants to compare prices, while half mentioned they used the tools to browse.

    As such, marketers are paying close attention to search, Merklin noted. She mentioned Tinuiti clients were expected to spend 11 to 15% more with Google compared with last year, with total search spending up 11% versus 2025. Clients’ standalone display campaign spending had largely shifted into the tech giant’s Demand Gen and Performance Max campaigns, which rose 30% and both include display and video inventory.

    PMG’s Carson noted clients were spending on social as well, with an eye to influencing product discovery, while also increasing CTV investments. “That’s an area where we expect investment to be up well into the double digits year-over-year,” she said.

    According to recent reports, “[It’s] something I don’t see slowing down in 2027,” addedCarson. “More advanced targeting capabilities here, including around placing ads during specific content contexts, are going to make it easier for brands to further invest.”.

    Meta’s reported CTV expansion and AppLovin’s alleged interest in Criteo are foreboding for independent ad tech as major platforms extend their reach.

    HUMAN Security’s latest investigation queries the effectiveness of CTV verification safeguards.

    In a recent development, the shift has been playing for the best part of a decade. COMvergence’s first Global Advertiser Survey shows how far its got.

    According to recent reports, “Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency and underlying health of the brand is giving us real confidence in the brand’s ability to continue its momentum,” said Gap Inc. CEO Richard Dickson on Thursday’s earnings call. “Our customer file continues to grow, particularly as we attract newer Gen Z customers, but we’re doing it while we’re preserving the brand’s multi-generational appeal.”.

    Industry observers note that dickson cited additional introduces from Gap’s collaborations with Hailey Bieber and Victoria Beckham as boosting sales in the period, along with the brand’s reentry into the beauty category. The company did not share specific figures from the revival of Gap’s classic ‘90s fragrances like Grass and Dream in July, but called the early response “encouraging.”.

    In a recent development, the tech giant is doubling down on creating what it calls “fashiontainment,” Dickson shared. Following the appointment of Pam Kaufman as evp, chief entertainment officer in January, Gap Inc. has tapped boy band Just Your Type (JYT) for a multi-year partnership and launched “The Agency,” a scripted microseries made for Banana Republic. Looking ahead, Dickson remarked Gap will also co-produce a docuseries.

    “We see our fashiontainment platform as a recognized way of how customers aren’t just buying apparel today; they’re buying into brands that are telling compelling stories and driving cultural conversations,” said Dickson.

    Gap is far from the only brand to attempt to extend its cultural relevance through entertainment. Gap collaborator and founder of her namesake brand Victoria Beckham was the subject of a 2025 docuseries made with Netflix and Studio 99, her husband David Beckham’s production organization. Maybelline launched a Christmas-themed “microdrama” in 2025, while shows like “Nobody Wants This” have featured a growing level of product placement with the likes of Estée Lauder and La Bonne Brosse.

    Walmart is allowing access to Meta’s Muse through a gateway that lets it control how AI agents browse, shop and make purchases.

    Amazon is paying to reach ChatGPT shoppers while the chatbot is finding other ways to surface its products and deals.

    Holiday marketing is changing: CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026.

    #89544. The Analog Advantage: Luxury Retail in the Age of AI at Bucherer

    The Analog Advantage: Luxury Retail in the Age of AI at Bucherer

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, no one needs a mechanical watch, but then again, luxury is not a category built on need.
    • The value comes from everything surrounding the object: scarcity, craftsmanship, identity, memory, access, and the community someone enters by owning it.
    • On this episode of The Speed of Culture podcast, Carina Ertl, chief marketing officer at Bucherer USA, joins Matt Britton to explore how those forces shape modern luxury marketing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, no one needs a mechanical watch, but then again, luxury is not a category built on need. And that is exactly what makes the marketing challenge interesting.

    The value comes from everything surrounding the object: scarcity, craftsmanship, identity, memory, access, and the community someone enters by owning it.

    On this episode of The Speed of Culture podcast, Carina Ertl, chief marketing officer at Bucherer USA, joins Matt Britton to explore how those forces shape modern luxury marketing.

    Their conversation examines why the category often reverses traditional demand economics, and how experience creates loyalty long after the purchase.

    The also discuss why passionate curators can outperform creators with massive followings, and why AI may make human taste an even stronger competitive advantage.

    Recent findings suggest that carina Ertl is the Chief Marketing Officer at Bucherer USA, part of the Swiss luxury watch and jewelry retailer whose heritage dates back to 1888. Bucherer operates across physical retail and ecommerce, offering luxury timepieces and jewelry.

    Recent findings suggest that carina’s career spans luxury brand building, digital transformation, entrepreneurship, private equity, and nearly a decade at Swarovski. Her experience across markets and business models has shaped an approach to marketing built around curiosity, cultural fluency, and long-term client relationships.

    According to recent reports, 02:52 Luxury Flips the Demand Curve — Carina describes luxury marketing as “art and science,” with perhaps a little more art than science. Unlike many categories trying to create demand, luxury often deals with the opposite problem: too much demand for too little product. That scarcity changes the marketing playbook. The goal, now, is to protect desirability while deepening the meaning surrounding the product.

    06:39 Certified Pre-Owned Turns Trust Into Value — The secondary watch market is growing, but Carina draws a sharp distinction between generic resale and certified pre-owned. Authentication matters because counterfeiting creates real uncertainty in the category. Certification gives consumers confidence while allowing retailers to unlock the history and storytelling embedded in older pieces, turning resale into its own desirable luxury experience.

    11:53 Between Product and Sale: Where the Real Product Lies — For Bucherer, the customer journey does not move directly from product to transaction. Carina sees the experience in between as part of the product itself: community, belonging, identity, storytelling, trust, and eventually repurchase. That makes luxury a long-term relationship business rather than a sequence of isolated sales.

    Industry observers note that 14:27 Trust Always Beats Follower Count — Carina says some of Bucherer’s strongest creator partnerships come from passionate curators rather than influencers with millions of followers. A smaller voice with deep category knowledge and a highly engaged community can carry more credibility than broad reach alone. Therein lies a major lesson for marketers: authority and authentic passion can matter more than audience size.

    In a recent development, 17:36 AI Makes Human Taste More Valuable — Carina is enthusiastic about AI as a productivity and process tool, but she sees a limit when automation starts replacing cultural judgment. In luxury, anyone can copy a formula. The differentiators are taste, creativity, execution, and knowing what is happening in culture and subculture. As AI makes generic ideas easier to generate, the distinctly human parts of brand building become more important.

    21:44 Curiosity Survives Every Marketing Shift — Carina’s advice to future marketing leaders is built around adaptability. Marketing has changed repeatedly throughout her career, from digital transformation to AI, and she does not believe anyone can graduate knowing everything they will need. The durable advantage is curiosity: seek unfamiliar projects, learn the broader business, and stay willing to change as the function changes around you.

    Recent findings suggest that matt Britton is America’s leading expert on the millennial generation having consulted for over half of the Fortune 500 over the past two decades. He is the Founder and CEO of Suzy and the host of The Speed of Culture Podcast.

    #89543. Breaking: The Rundown: BADBOX 3.0, the CTV ad fraud scheme generating 40 billion bid requests a day

    Breaking: The Rundown: BADBOX 3.0, the CTV ad fraud scheme generating 40 billion bid requests a day

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Last week, HUMAN Security claimed it has disrupted the largest publicly disclosed ad fraud operation by bid-request volume, uncovering a network of infected streaming devices generating up to 40 billion fraudulent ad requests daily.
    • Dubbed “BADBOX 3.0,” the scheme accounted for more than 4% of CTV traffic observed by HUMAN, using compromised Android TV boxes to impersonate legitimate streaming apps and generate advertising activity without viewers’ knowledge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Last week, HUMAN Security claimed it has disrupted the largest publicly disclosed ad fraud operation by bid-request volume, uncovering a network of infected streaming devices generating up to 40 billion fraudulent ad requests daily.

    Dubbed “BADBOX 3.0,” the scheme accounted for more than 4% of CTV traffic observed by HUMAN, using compromised Android TV boxes to impersonate legitimate streaming apps and generate advertising activity without viewers’ knowledge.

    The Nov. 18 disclosure raises fresh questions about the effectiveness of CTV ad fraud detection — and how much fraudulent inventory slips through existing safeguards, crucial gaps for the industry to collectively plug as marketers increasingly spend ad dollars on such channels.

    According to HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence team, the situation involved a network of compromised, low-cost Android-based streaming devices running malware designed to generate fraudulent video advertising activity without their owners’ knowledge.

    The operation was more than three times larger, by peak daily bid-request volume, than VASTFLUX, previously the largest publicly disclosed scheme measured on that basis.

    Researchers linked elements of the malware distribution infrastructure to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, identifying connections involving device software, code repositories and command-and-control servers.

    HUMAN also uncovered links to earlier BADBOX operations, including BADBOX 2.0, which was exposed in 2025 and involved more than 10 million compromised devices across 222 countries and territories.

    The latest discovery illustrates how fraud operations can reconstitute themselves following earlier disruptions, adapting their infrastructure and techniques to evade detection.

    The malware then installed advertising software on infected devices, allowing video commercials to play in hidden windows while users continued watching television or navigating their streaming interfaces.

    The resulting advertising requests impersonated legitimate CTV applications, making the inventory appear authentic to downstream buyers.

    Some fraudulent requests also originated from residential proxy networks, helping disguise their source as ordinary household internet traffic.

    Sources indicate that HUMAN identified 11 proxy networks in which compromised devices could be enrolled without their owners’ consent, effectively turning consumer internet connections into infrastructure available for third-party use. Separately, researchers uncovered spoofed server-side ad insertion traffic, in which fraudulent requests purported to represent advertisements inserted into streaming sessions that did not actually exist.

    The scale of the operation is considerable, although its financial impact remains unclear.

    Crucially, the 40 billion figure represents bid requests, not completed advertising transactions or billable impressions. Consequently, it cannot be used to calculate advertiser losses without establishing how much fraudulent inventory was purchased.

    Sources indicate that hence, the question remains: what proportion of the 40 billion daily bid requests became paid impressions? And how much money was spent on invalid inventory?

    However, due to the intricacies of online ad auctions – where CPMs can vary significantly – HUMAN was unable to provide an exact dollar amount when asked about the financial impact of the operation.

    Nonetheless, sources approached by Digiday estimated that BADBOX 3.0 could potentially have cost advertisers millions of dollars per day at its height.

    Shailin Dhar, partner at Futureproof TMT, cautioned against equating the operation’s 40 billion daily bid requests with actual advertiser losses, noting that CTV supply audited by his firm since 2024 has averaged a fill rate of approximately 2%. He further counseled that fraudulent inventory originating from low-end applications and devices could perform considerably worse.

    Industry observers note that at this juncture, it’s worth considering that enormous volumes of fraudulent auction traffic do not necessarily translate into equivalent volumes of wasted advertising expenditure. At an illustrative fill rate of 0.5% and realized revenue of $3 per thousand impressions, 40 billion daily requests would generate approximately $600,000 in revenue. However, Dhar stressed that such calculations should not be mistaken for evidence of the operation’s actual earnings.

    Nevertheless, the operation’s ability to masquerade as legitimate streaming inventory highlights potential weaknesses in how CTV advertising transactions are authenticated.

    Sources indicate that CTV has become an increasingly notable channel for advertisers seeking to reach audiences migrating from traditional television. However, its programmatic infrastructure also presents opportunities for fraudsters to exploit fragmented supply paths and inconsistent verification practices.

    Industry observers note that BADBOX 3.0 demonstrates how apparently legitimate app identifiers, residential IP addresses and video ad requests can be combined to manufacture the appearance of genuine viewing activity. The question is whether existing safeguards can consistently identify such behavior before advertisers are charged.

    Futureproof’s Dhar questioned the effectiveness of existing verification safeguards, arguing that private marketplaces and curated deals remain vulnerable because of limited device, content, and connection signals, alongside excessive confidence in identity matching.

    “My personal estimate is roughly a 90% chance that at least one comparable operation is running without public identification,” he told Digiday, while acknowledging that its scale and financial impact remain unknown.

    Per Dhar’s assessment, effective CTV verification requires persistent checks throughout the advertising supply chain, rather than relying exclusively on pre-bid or post-bid detection.

    For now, HUMAN indicates customers using its Ad Fraud Defense service are protected against the operation’s associated attacks, while its researchers continue monitoring the perpetrators for further adaptations.

    The findings come roughly a month after a separate investigation by ad security firm Confiant and researchers at Citizen Lab exposed how online advertising infrastructure was used to distribute spyware, highlighting another vulnerability in the digital advertising ecosystem.

    That investigation, detailed in research published by Citizen Lab, found that Israeli company Discover-Tech exploited targeted advertising mechanisms to deliver zero-click spyware, including attacks against devices at Al Jazeera.

    While the two operations differed in their objectives — one targeting advertising budgets, the other facilitating surveillance — both illustrate how infrastructure designed to connect advertisers with audiences can be repurposed for malicious activity.

    The broader concern is that BADBOX 3.0 is another iteration of an established threat rather than an isolated incident — and that dismantling one operation does not necessarily eliminate the infrastructure or incentives behind the next.

    Meta’s reported CTV expansion and AppLovin’s alleged interest in Criteo are foreboding for independent ad tech as major platforms extend their reach.

    Advertisers continue to increase investments on the retail weekend but AI, tariffs and discounting pressure present banana skins.

    The shift has been playing for the best part of a decade. COMvergence’s first Global Advertiser Survey shows how far its got.

    D+ Research: Brand’s holiday marketing tactics shift in 2026

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders.
    • According to recent reports, this is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →.

    According to recent reports, this is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies. The report is based on a survey of 90 brand and retailer professionals, as well as individual interviews with marketing executives.

    Digiday’s survey found that brands and retailers blueprint to adjust the marketing tactics they’ll use during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to those they used in 2025.

    The biggest changes are that CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026, with year-over-year increases of 22 percentage points and 20 percentage points, respectively.

    Sources indicate that forty-five percent of survey respondents said they proposal to use CTV/streaming ads this holiday season, in comparison to 23% of respondents who said the same in 2025. The 2026 uptick followed a 14 percentage point dip in usage from 2024 to 2025.Meanwhile, marketers’ usage of TV ads remained relatively stable between 2024 and 2025, dropping by only 4 percentage points between 2024 and 2025, but grew by a whopping 20 percentage points in 2026. Thirty-three percent of brands and retailers said they plan to use TV ads this holiday season in comparison to 13% of marketers who said the same in 2025.

    “Streaming is a really valid channel to invest in during holiday because consumption of that media spikes,” stated Laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement manufacturer Ritual. “But participating in streaming is actually a decision for the whole year. Starting to engage just for holiday would be a risky move, especially for a smaller brand.”.

    “If you have the data to back it up over the course of the year showing this is a channel that’s proven and the ROI metrics associated, it can make a lot of sense to spike it during holiday,” she added.

    It has been revealed that ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, stated that both streaming and TV ads can be effective for targeting specific demographic groups during the holidays. “Streaming and television is an effective audience conversion mechanism, especially with women over 30 years old,” Bloom said. “We’ve done a lot of work on daytime TV and on QVC. We see significantly bigger segments in the holiday time period from November through mid-December, and we always put attention on those times.”.

    Last year, brands’ and retailers’ most-used holiday marketing tactic was brand experiences, but that strategy fell to second place in 2026 behind streaming/CTV ads. Forty-one percent of marketers noted they expect to use brand experiences as a marketing strategy during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to 50% of marketers who said the same in 2025 — a drop of 9 percentage points.

    According to recent reports, brands and retailers are also divesting from using gift guides and influencer hauls/unboxing videos this holiday season. Marketers’ usage of gift guides decreased by 19 percentage points in 2026 vs. 2025, while their use of influencer hauls/unboxing videos fell by 14 percentage points this year in comparison to last year.

    Although gift guides and brand experiences decreased in marketer usage for the 2026 holidays, they remain brands’ and retailers’ top performing holiday marketing tactics over time. Thirty-one percent of marketers stated gift guides have historically performed the best for their company during the holiday season, while 28% of marketers said the same of brand experiences, putting them in the No. 1 and No. 2 ranking spots, respectively.

    Although some marketers are shifting away from using gift guides for the upcoming holiday season, Ritual’s Brodie said gift guides are likely to gain importance in the AI-driven search era because AI-powered search tools often rely on best of lists and curated recommendations to answer consumer queries.

    In a recent development, “Gift guides are very interesting in the world of AEO and thinking about LLM optimization,” Brodie said. “Overall, best of lists and gift guides are a close sister to [AI search results]. Gift guides can play an notable role in holiday and especially bridging LLM research and AI overviews. So, I’m bullish about gift guides.”.

    Recent findings suggest that although brands and retailers are leaning into CTV/streaming ads for the 2026 holidays, those marketing tactics tied in the No. 4 spot for the best-performing holiday marketing tactic over time, while pop-up shops ranked No. 3. Influencer hauls/unboxing videos was the only marketing strategy that fell in both best historic performance and marketers’ intended use during the 2026 holiday season.

    Recent findings suggest that A-Frame Brands’ Bloom stated brands and retailers should also consider investing in catalogs for the 2026 holiday. “Catalogs have always been very successful, and they’re heavily conversion-focused,” Bloom explained. “When they’re discount-driven and when people’s attention is on buying, you can do offers that you can only get via physical paper, and it does drive people into stores.”.

    Walmart is allowing access to Meta’s Muse through a gateway that lets it control how AI agents browse, shop and make purchases.

    Amazon is paying to reach ChatGPT shoppers while the chatbot is finding other ways to surface its products and deals.

    Sources indicate that gap Inc. has tapped boy band Just Your Type (JYT) for a multi-year partnership and debuted “The Agency,” a scripted microseries made for Banana Republic.

    Agencies are selling AI efficiency — clients want outcomes

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Sources indicate that agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story.
    • Recent findings suggest that that is not an AI problem.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Amol Waishampayan, co-founder, fullthrottle.ai.

    Sources indicate that agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story. Faster work, leaner teams, lower fees. Clients took the meeting, nodded along and then waited for the invoice to shrink. It didn’t. AI strategies now sound interchangeable to clients, who say the savings never showed up in their fees.

    Recent findings suggest that that is not an AI problem. It is a positioning problem. Efficiency was the wrong promise. Clients do not hire agencies to be fast. They hire them to grow the business. AI’s real opportunity for agencies is not doing the same work cheaper. It is doing work that actually moves revenue, and proving it.

    It has been revealed that agencies are getting operational value from AI. According to the Digiday Media Agency Report 2026, 70% of agencies say AI has cut costs by making tasks more efficient, while 31% say it cost more to implement than expected. But efficiency is a one-time gain.

    Once every agency has it, nobody gets paid for it. As one Gartner analyst told Digiday, the honeymoon between agencies and AI is “essentially over.” The agencies that build their AI story on productivity are competing on margin. The ones that build it on performance are competing on value, and value is what clients renew.

    Most media prepares are still organized by channel. Search budget here, social budget there, streaming over in a separate deck. AI makes that structure obsolete, because it can proposal around the customer instead.

    Industry observers note that take a regional home services company running paid search and social. Those campaigns are producing something more valuable than clicks: a live stream of households actively researching its services. AI can turn those signals into a defined first-party audience, figure out where else those households spend their time, and extend the blueprint into streaming TV, digital video and audio to reach them there. One audience, coordinated across channels, built from the client’s own demand rather than a platform’s inventory.

    It has been revealed that that is a different kind of planning. The question stops being “what should we spend on CTV” and becomes “who are we trying to reach, and where are they?”.

    Sources indicate that the next step is letting AI act on that intelligence. Agentic systems can take audience and performance signals and adjust targeting, channel mix and spend as conditions change, instead of waiting for the monthly optimization meeting. Static aims with quarterly reviews are a relic of how long it used to take humans to read the data.

    But here is where agencies should be careful. The advantage is not how much of the buying you automate. Anyone can automate. The advantage is whether the agent is optimizing toward something that matters. An agent chasing cheaper CPMs will find them, and the client will not care. An agent optimizing toward the client’s actual business outcomes, with the agency keeping full transparency and control, is a different product entirely.

    In a recent development, this is the part most of the industry still avoids. Clicks and impressions are easy to report and nearly impossible to defend in a budget conversation. The only metrics a CFO cares about are sales, customers and revenue.

    Recent findings suggest that AI makes closing that gap practical. Bring together the advertiser’s first-party customer data, its transaction history and campaign exposure, and one can see which households were reached, which ones became customers and which channels and audiences did the work. Done with privacy-first, household-level methods rather than individual tracking, this is not surveillance. It is the client’s own data finally answering the client’s own question.

    Recent findings suggest that once that loop exists, everything upstream improves. Planning gets smarter because it is fed by real conversions. Agentic buying gets better because it is optimizing toward revenue instead of proxies. And the agency walks into every renewal with proof rather than a deck.

    Agencies are already monetizing AI. Digiday’s report found that 59% are launching newly introduced AI-powered products, 34% are selling strategic roadmaps or audits and 31% are charging additional fees for AI-powered services. But if the product is “we have AI,” the pricing power will not last. Every competitor has AI. Within a year, every client will have it too.

    In a recent development, the agencies that win the next cycle will not be the ones with the most AI. They will be the ones who can show a client exactly what it delivered, in the client’s own numbers. Efficiency gets agencies a thank-you. Outcomes get agencies the next three years of the account.Partner insights from fullthrottle.ai.

    The next test for agentic media

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, join us Dec.
    • Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory.
    • Advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory.

    Advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work. These teams have their own agents, their own data and their own rules for what an agent may and may not do. At the same time, most of the specialized intelligence they depend on still sits inside separate vendor platforms.

    As a result, vendor intelligence shapes a recommendation while remaining disconnected from the system acting on the recommendation. When planners carry conclusions between tools, the evidence and conditions behind those recommendations often fall away.

    Sources indicate that that’s the problem agentic media has to solve next. Can the intelligence behind the agent go where the work happens?

    Models and agent frameworks are widely available. Two vendors can build on the same foundation and ship agents that look identical in a demo. What separates them is what the agent knows, and whether the advertiser can put that knowledge to work. In media buying, that knowledge is specific.

    It has been revealed that A broad content classification offers only a starting point for a media decision. Suitability depends on the particular advertiser and market, and those judgments can change quickly when breaking news alters the significance of a placement. A general-purpose model can’t reconstruct that brand-specific knowledge or historical context from a prompt alone. Classification depth and performance history can.

    For Channel Factory, that means IAB 3.0 classification across more than 15 million YouTube channels, and more than 10 years and $4 billion of campaign performance data. To be clear, this isn’t an argument for keeping that intelligence locked inside a platform; it’s the opposite. Intelligence that only works inside its owner’s interface is as limited as a capable agent no one can reach.

    According to recent reports, so the test is portability. Can an advertiser’s own agent call on a provider’s intelligence directly, from inside the planning and buying environment it already uses? That’s how Channel Factory is building, with contextual and suitability intelligence made available through APIs and MCP servers, and delivered through modular agents that run inside an advertiser’s environment or alongside it.

    With this architecture, market-specific suitability analysis becomes part of an advertiser’s own planning process. An agent can evaluate inventory against the provider’s classifications and historical performance data, applying the relevant standards for each market. Those findings can directly inform the strategy, with the advertiser’s existing rules governing what the agent can recommend or change.

    Recent findings suggest that portable intelligence doesn’t mean identical agents. Two advertisers can draw on the same underlying intelligence and make different decisions. For instance, one avoids content when signals are unclear while another favors reaching inside defined boundaries. Both are valid because the thresholds, priorities and approval rules are the advertisers’.

    Sources indicate that an agent’s knowledge source shouldn’t determine the scope of its authority. The brand decides what acceptable judgment looks like. The provider keeps the classification, history and models current.

    Learning needs the same discipline. Feedback and outcomes should refine recommendations, but advertisers should decide what shapes future decisions and which policies stay fixed. On its own, a successful campaign shouldn’t rewrite a brand’s suitability standards.

    According to recent reports, intelligence that moves into someone else’s systems has to carry its accountability along. As agents shift from recommending to acting, teams need to see what changed, why and whether it stayed within approved limits.

    Recent findings suggest that the principle is simple: Agents do the reasoning, and the engine owns the state, so every action is authorized, logged and traceable to the signals behind it. People define the strategy. Autonomy is earned in stages: alerts first, then recommendations, then bounded actions. An agent might make a small budget adjustment under set conditions while sending a larger change for human approval. How much authority to delegate is the advertiser’s call, and the system should make that call easy to enforce and easy to review.

    Industry observers note that as agentic capabilities spread, feature lists will converge. Advertisers should look underneath the interface and put three questions to any provider:.

    The providers who can answer those clearly will matter more as brands take greater control of how they buy media. The rest will be unrealized demos.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, join us Dec.
    • Amazon is paying OpenAI to reach the same shoppers it refuses to let ChatGPT study.
    • After a relatively quiet few months on the chatbot following its Prime Day activity, the e-commerce giant has returned to the platform with a new round of Black Friday ads in the U.S., Digiday has seen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Amazon is paying OpenAI to reach the same shoppers it refuses to let ChatGPT study.

    After a relatively quiet few months on the chatbot following its Prime Day activity, the e-commerce giant has returned to the platform with a new round of Black Friday ads in the U.S., Digiday has seen.

    The ads, which are the same format as typical ChatGPT ads — separate from the user conversation, with a favicon, headline, description and a “Learn more” call to action — are appearing in ChatGPT in the lead-up to Black Friday. They promote Amazon Black Friday deals and direct customers to Amazon to complete their purchases.

    What’s different compared to other retailers, though, is how ChatGPT is surfacing Amazon products and deals. Rather than directing users to individual product pages, ChatGPT’s shopping experience is linking to Amazon search results, while drawing on third-party deal-tracking websites to identify products, discounts and up-to-date pricing. That means ChatGPT can help consumers discover Amazon products and compare deals without necessarily accessing Amazon’s own website directly.

    Amazon’s increased activity on ChatGPT is interesting given the retailer already operates its own shopping ecosystem and one of the world’s largest ad businesses. Its presence on the chatbot puts it in the position of using a competing platform to drive shoppers back to its own marketplace, while that same platform is developing its own way of facilitating product discovery around Amazon’s catalogue.

    Amazon also has an opportunity to monetize that traffic once shoppers arrive on its marketplace.

    “Sending shoppers to Amazon search results rather than individual product pages also creates another opportunity to make money from advertising,” noted Arielle Feger, senior analyst, commerce media and retail at eMarketer.

    It has been revealed that amazon’s U.S. search ad revenues are forecasted to reach $40.57 billion this year, nearly a quarter of all U.S. search ad spending. Traffic coming from ChatGPT gives Amazon another opportunity to put sponsored products in front of shoppers.

    Sources indicate that “For brands, that creates a risk of paying twice for the same customer,” Feger added. “Even after winning a recommendation in ChatGPT, a brand could find itself paying again to compete against sponsored listings on Amazon.”.

    But Amazon’s relationship with ChatGPT extends beyond buying ad space for its own products.

    Recent findings suggest that in September, Amazon Ads revealed a partnership with OpenAI that allows advertisers to buy ChatGPT inventory through Amazon’s DSP, extending their existing Amazon ad campaigns onto the chatbot. The integration initially gives select U.S. advertisers access to ChatGPT’s ad inventory through Amazon DSP, giving brands another route to reach consumers using the AI chatbot.

    What is unclear is whether Amazon has bought its ChatGPT ads directly from OpenAI, or through its own DSP.

    Both Amazon and OpenAI declined to comment on this article.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Retail media is no longer just about putting products in front of shoppers and measuring the resulting sales.

    As the retail landscape becomes increasingly complex, brands need to rethink how they connect with consumers across the entire shopper journey.

    The opportunity lies in building connected campaigns that bring together shopper insights, creative strategy, and coordinated experiences across digital, social, and in-store touchpoints.

    In this episode of Adspeak by ADWEEK, host Zoë Ruderman sits down with Liz Roche, VP of media, measurement, and in-store solutions at Albertsons Media Collective, to explore how brands and retailers can move beyond traditional retail media strategies to create more meaningful shopper connections.

    They discuss why understanding shopper missions and need states matters more than simply showcasing products, and why shopper data should inform creative development from the very beginning of a campaign.

    It has been revealed that the conversation examines what makes a genuinely connected campaign. Rather than repeating the same message across multiple channels, brands need to understand where shoppers are in their journey and build experiences that reflect their immediate needs.

    Liz explains how seemingly ordinary purchase signals can reveal valuable shopper insights, helping marketers understand the motivations behind buying behavior and make smarter decisions about creative, SKU selection, and promotional strategy.

    They also explore the importance of moving beyond vanity metrics like return on ad spend. By combining incrementality, category insights, and brand performance, marketers can develop more meaningful measurement frameworks that demonstrate the true impact of retail media.

    The discussion also looks at the untapped potential of the physical store as a media canvas, from in-store screens to audio experiences that can extend brand storytelling beyond traditional advertising.

    Liz Roche is the VP of Media, Measurement & In-Store Solutions at Albertsons Media Collective. A seasoned executive, she specializes in first-party data strategy, media measurement, monetization, commercialization, and go-to-market strategy.

    With leadership experience spanning platforms, agencies, and publishers, Liz drives business transformation through innovation, strategic partnerships, and collaboration. She holds an Executive MBA from the Kellogg School of Management, where she was honored as the commencement speaker in June 2024.

    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m.
    • AppLovin’s reported interest in Criteo and Meta’s intends to explore CTV could put further pressure on independent ad tech, with some companies reporting challenging circumstances in the latest round of earnings calls.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    AppLovin’s reported interest in Criteo and Meta’s intends to explore CTV could put further pressure on independent ad tech, with some companies reporting challenging circumstances in the latest round of earnings calls.

    Last week, Reuters reported unconfirmed acquisition discussions involving AppLovin and Criteo, the same day Next in Media reported that Meta was exploring partnerships with television manufacturers and free FAST services to extend its advertising platform into CTV.

    If both sets of developments materialize, it would represent two of the largest established (mobile) ad platforms expanding into fresh channels using existing advertiser relationships, data, and buying technology.

    It’s well understood that AppLovin wants to extend its performance advertising business beyond mobile applications, and Criteo — a tech giant that is reportedly seeking an exit from the public markets — could provide retail relationships, commerce data, and access to advertisers across the open web.

    Meanwhile, Meta could use its existing buying platform to help advertisers reach television audiences without relying on a separate demand-side platform.

    In recent weeks, separate sources told Digiday this could prove a key advantage in helping the social networking outfit eat into Google’s lead in markets where its DSP, DV 360, dominates.

    However, developments could reduce advertisers’ dependence on independent DSPs and supply-side platforms.

    AppLovin’s potential shortcut into commerce.

    Private equity firms Vista Equity Partners and Quinti Capital have also reportedly expressed interest in Criteo, which has engaged an investment bank to evaluate its options.

    AppLovin reported third-quarter revenue of $2.19 billion, up 55% year over year, alongside $1.44 billion in net income.

    Criteo reported a 12% revenue decline to $416 million, with net income falling to approximately $6 million.

    AppLovin’s growth has been driven by mobile advertising, although the manufacturer is increasingly targeting e-commerce advertisers outside of gaming.

    Criteo has spent years expanding beyond retargeting into commerce media, developing relationships with retailers, access to shopper data and cross-channel advertising capabilities.

    Per official figures, Criteo’s commerce intelligence draws on more than $1 trillion in annual transactions, 740 million daily active users and over 5 billion product SKUs, and acquiring it could accelerate AppLovin’s expansion into retail media, providing relationships and data it would otherwise need to develop independently.

    However, integrating the businesses would be complicated given that AppLovin’s core technology is built around mobile apps, while Criteo operates across retailers, publishers, and other commerce environments.

    The potential benefits would depend on whether their different data assets, buying systems, and commercial relationships could work effectively when integrated.

    Earlier in the year, multiple sources told Digiday that Meta is ⁠exploring an option that would allow advertisers to extend campaigns into third-party television inventory through its existing advertising tools — a measurement tactic commonly known as audience extension.

    The latest reporting suggests Meta is considering how those relationships could support an advertiser-facing buying option, resembling Pinterest’s CTV audience-extension offering, which lets advertisers use Pinterest’s audience data to reach consumers beyond its owned properties. Meta could pursue a similar approach at considerably greater scale.

    Its existing advertiser base could access television inventory without establishing separate relationships with specialist CTV buying platforms, an attractive option for smaller advertisers already using Meta’s automated campaign tools.

    For DSPs and SSPs, the competitive implications would be significant, as Meta could bring more advertisers directly into CTV, potentially reducing the role of intermediaries that connect buyers with television inventory.

    It has been revealed that but questions remain about how the proposed model would operate. For example, would Meta determine which inventory advertisers purchase? Plus, how would fees and media costs be disclosed? And what independent measurement would be available?

    Such details are likely to determine whether Meta’s proposed offering creates a meaningful alternative to existing CTV buying arrangements or simply adds another layer between advertisers and publishers.

    AppLovin’s interest in Criteo and Meta’s reported CTV expansion reflect a broader shift in advertising technology, as larger companies with bigger advertiser bases and proprietary data extend their buying capabilities into additional channels. Amazon is pursuing a similar strategy through its DSP and retail media business, which is morphing into a unified agentic platform.

    Sources indicate that the Trade Desk’s recent financial performance illustrates the difficulties facing some independent players. The tech giant reported a 0.5% third-quarter revenue decline to $736 million, marking a rare contraction after years of sustained growth, and is on course to simplify and offer new measurement capabilities as it attempts to restore growth.

    While The Trade Desk’s recent revenue decline cannot be attributed to Meta’s reported plans or AppLovin’s potential acquisition, the contrast provides context for broader competitive pressure on independent buying platforms.

    The emergence of unified media platforms is another response, as ⁠last week’s explainer outlined; these systems aim to coordinate advertising across search, social, programmatic, and direct publisher relationships.

    Industry observers note that but coordinating buying across platforms is not the same as controlling the underlying inventory, data, or optimization technology. Independent companies will need to demonstrate value beyond simplifying workflows, particularly as AI makes campaign execution easier.

    For independent ad tech, maintaining a meaningful role in that environment will become increasingly difficult.

    Figures from ⁠HUMAN Security’s BADBOX 3.0 investigation, published Nov. 18.

    ⁠WTF is a unified media platform?

    The industry’s emerging buying platforms promise to coordinate advertising across channels, but their ability to control actual spending decisions remains contested.

    ⁠Ad Tech Briefing: Google’s antitrust troubles aren’t over.

    Google’s European antitrust exposure and The Trade Desk’s financial difficulties illustrate the challenges facing established ad tech businesses.

    “Global Privacy Control (GPC) WebKit API, for all you browser and browsing experience developers out there.”.

    — John Wilander, Apple’s privacy frontman, introduces a software revision that will let app developers let users signal their preference to opt out of data sharing and cross-context targeted advertising, a right supported by regulations like the CCPA.

    ⁠Anthropic claims no to ads, but Wall Street may have other ideas.

    Anthropic’s opposition to advertising raises questions about whether the tech giant can maintain that position as the cost of developing and operating AI models increases.

    ⁠Ampersand is offloading its indie agency business to Comcast and Spectrum following mass layoffs.

    Ampersand’s restructuring and the transfer of its independent agency business to Comcast and Spectrum highlight the pressures facing traditional television advertising intermediaries.

    ⁠AI-driven tech layoffs suck, but might lead to certification.

    Jonathan Bellack examines how AI coding tools are reducing opportunities for junior engineers, and considers whether professional certification could help establish new standards for software development.

    ⁠Tech companies are trying to shift the entire concept of privacy again.

    The Electronic Frontier Foundation examines how technology companies are attempting to redefine privacy protections as AI systems create newly introduced opportunities to collect and process personal information.

    HUMAN Security’s latest investigation queries the effectiveness of CTV verification safeguards.

    Advertisers continue to increase investments on the retail weekend but AI, tariffs and discounting pressure present banana skins.

    Industry observers note that the shift has been playing for the best part of a decade. COMvergence’s first Global Advertiser Survey shows how far its got.

    Walmart is letting Meta’s Muse shop its shelves — but on its own terms

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, join us Dec.
    • By letting Meta’s Muse agent into its stores only through the gateway it built and controls, Walmart is treating AI agent access the way retail media networks once treated ad slots: as inventory to be doled out on its own terms.
    • The retailer is preparing to launch a connector to Muse that will provide the AI agent with defined access to its e-commerce infrastructure, meaning it gets to set the guardrails and boundaries within which Meta’s agent can browse and shop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    By letting Meta’s Muse agent into its stores only through the gateway it built and controls, Walmart is treating AI agent access the way retail media networks once treated ad slots: as inventory to be doled out on its own terms.

    The retailer is preparing to launch a connector to Muse that will provide the AI agent with defined access to its e-commerce infrastructure, meaning it gets to set the guardrails and boundaries within which Meta’s agent can browse and shop.

    The capability was noticed by Juozas Kaziukėnas, founder of e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, after he spotted an upgrade to Walmart’s technical instruction manual for Muse. According to The Verge, that integration introduces tomorrow (Nov. 24), in time for Black Friday Cyber Monday shopping.

    In a recent development, the manual, which Digiday has also seen and verified, describes how Muse can interact with Walmart’s shopping systems on behalf of a user. This includes tasks like searching for products, answering questions, building shopping carts and, if permission is granted, completing orders. Muse can also call on Walmart’s own shopping assistant Sparky to answer questions about products, stores and comparisons.

    So a Walmart Shopper could ask Muse to compare three televisions, find specific ingredients for a dinner party, or ask the agent to add products to its Walmart shopping cart. Muse can then use Walmart’s systems to carry out those tasks. For example, Walmart could help Muse identify a customer’s usual brand of milk without handing over their entire shopping history.

    Recent findings suggest that this goes beyond what someone might typically expect from a chatbot, where a user might simply ask for recommendations. Instead, Muse, through the gateway to Walmart’s own marketplace, can act on those recommendations, taking care of the legwork involved in shopping and even making purchases once the user has given the necessary permission.

    Walmart talked about its vision for this in its blog post last month.

    Built using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the integration gives AI agents a more direct and reliable way to interact with Walmart’s shopping systems. It’s designed to let agents shop on a customer’s behalf without giving them access to their wider purchase history or unnecessary personal information. For example, Walmart could help Muse identify a customer’s usual brand of milk without handing over their entire shopping history.

    In a recent development, walmart has also started introducing Agent Profiles, which gives each AI agent its own dedicated profile within a customer’s Walmart account. It means shoppers can distinguish purchases made by an AI agent from the ones they’ve completed themselves, while deciding how much autonomy they want to give the agent. Customers can require approval for every purchase, or set a spending limit (such as $50, $100 or $200), allowing the agent to spend up to that amount without seeking approval each time. Customers also have the ability to disable the agent’s access at any time.

    Sources indicate that this development comes after Amazon already blocked Muse from accessing its e-commerce site in September, arguing that third-party AI agents should operate openly and respect retailers’ decisions about whether to participate. At the time, Amazon remarked it asked Meta to remove its website from Muse’s shopping experience, but Meta declined. It also raised concerns about Muse accessing customer accounts without authorization and potentially capturing customer credentials. However, Meta disputed the claims, saying Muse cannot see users’ passwords or payment details.

    While Walmart might be working closer with Muse going forward, this approach could raise questions about its ad business. In particular, with Muse increasingly allowed to take over product discovery, where does that leave its sponsored product placements and how much influence will brands have over what an AI agent recommends.

    In a recent development, “There will emerge a newly introduced advertising mechanism where brands will pay dollars not for a sponsored placement, but for a ‘sponsored consideration’ to the agents,” remarked Abhishek Bora, head of digital growth at All Star Elite. “If agents take over the buying process, how would a new brand with a better product and offer get considered by an agent when it has no history of reviews, usage or purchases?”.

    Neither Walmart nor Meta responded to Digiday’s request for comment.

    Amazon is paying to reach ChatGPT shoppers while the chatbot is finding other ways to surface its products and deals.

    Holiday marketing is changing: CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026.

    Gap Inc. has tapped boy band Just Your Type (JYT) for a multi-year partnership and launched “The Agency,” a scripted microseries made for Banana Republic.

    #89523. Breaking: Why brands are writing no-AI clauses into creator deals

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (687 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Why brands are writing no-AI clauses into creator deals

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Influencer marketing contracts have become a focal point in the creator economy.
    • “We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns,” said Kurt Stadelman, vp of talent at creator marketing firm Pearpop, in a conversation with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde during Digiday’s recent Creator Strategies event.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Influencer marketing contracts have become a focal point in the creator economy. There’s heightened attention being paid by brands, creators and creators’ representatives to deal terms, such as usage rights, exclusivity and payment terms. But among the newest addendums is AI usage.

    “We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns,” said Kurt Stadelman, vp of talent at creator marketing firm Pearpop, in a conversation with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde during Digiday’s recent Creator Strategies event.

    Creators are actually welcoming brands’ no-AI demands, he said. Creators are already concerned about generative AI being used to create content and crowd out creators from people’s feeds. So brands forbidding AI-generated content from creators signals a commitment by brands to human-made content, said Stadelman.

    Industry observers note that but what counts as AI-generated content? Does it prohibit the creator from using AI tools in any part of their process?

    Industry observers note that “We’ve had to specify that a few times just to make sure, because obviously you want the creator to be able to use AI tools in the background when they’re developing their concept or their script. Even utilizing AI to analyze their past performance of their content and advise them on their strategy moving forward. And I think brands should probably embrace that because it ultimately helps the creator deliver the best version of themselves and the best content possible,” stated Stadelman.

    Here are a few highlights from the conversation, which have been edited for length and clarity.

    Sources indicate that it’s way too risky to be only utilizing organic posting for creator campaigns and just hoping that the right people see it. We are seeing more and more brands utilize paid behind whether it’s white-listing or utilizing the creator content as an ad unit for themselves on their own channels. Along with that comes, obviously, you have to write the paid usage rights into the contract, and most brands are good about that.

    The wrong length for usage rights.

    In a recent development, usage in perpetuity should never be agreed to. That’s a dangerous place to be for a creator and can negatively impact their future collaborations with other brands in the same category. Exclusivity, obviously, is quite difficult for a lot of creators if they agree to a longer exclusivity term than they should. That limits their options moving forward.

    The right length for usage rights.

    Sources indicate that sometimes you’ll see proposed terms that are just a little too lengthy with the usage rights. We push back on that sometimes. I don’t think there’s any reason to be agreeing upfront to any more than six months of paid usage. Even that’s a bit lengthy. Starting it at three months if they’re really wanting to utilize paid with the campaign, that makes sense. Even up to six months is fine in most cases. But once you get to that point six months from now, you can reassess and extend if you’d like. But I don’t think there’s any reason to go beyond that in the initial contract.

    We always push for shorter payment terms. If somebody’s asking for net-90, we try to push for net-60 or, ideally, net-30. But I understand that some brands have their standard operating procedures there, which is fine. But we just ask that they honor those payment terms, which is a whole other issue that we’re seeing happen more and more, is that brands are just not honoring these payment terms that they’ve themselves written into the contract.

    Kentucky-based whiskey brand Evan Williams Bourbon has become the first sponsor in the distilled spirits category to secure a sponsorship position across Disney-owned ACC Network’s college football live games or studio broadcasts.

    This comes as Evan Williams and its ad agency, Method1, have partnered with the ACC and Big Ten as part of a broader national college football media initiative.

    In a statement, a Disney spokesperson noted Evan Williams is presently the only advertiser in this category with a presence on the ACC Network. The spokesperson added that while this could change as the season progresses, the deal does not include an official ACC Network designation, but “it further reinforces Evan Williams’ leadership position within the category and effectively cements the brand’s presence within the ACC Network college football ecosystem.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On November 17, The Rx Assistant, an AI-powered service that helps patients streamline the prescriptions process by finding doctors, verifying insurance coverage, and enrolling patients in savings programs, revealed the launch of Builder — a specialized platform for pharmaceutical brands to deliver AI experiences for patients.

    The Rx Assistant Builder is a no-code platform that enables pharmaceutical brands to rapidly create, get regulatory approval for, and deploy compliant AI patient and provider support tools across web, voice, SMS, and email.

    The aim of Builder was to further simplify the prescription process for both pharmaceutical manufacturers and patients. From a pharmaceutical brand standpoint, Builder helps gather different tools and processes into one place. The flexibility of user experience, such as being able to switch from online to voice chat, allows manufacturers to cater to different needs depending on different patient populations.

    According to recent reports, “AI, when deployed correctly, can decrease time wasted in the ‘healthcare consideration cycle.’” said Jake Coniglio, co-founder and CEO, The Rx Assistant. “This counter balancing force can simultaneously allow patients and HCPs to to source information faster and go deeper.”.

    In its early deployments, The Rx Assistant found that its AI assistant outperformed brands’ own websites on a 3 to 1 scale, on tasks such as finding doctors and completing symptom quizzes. Brands were also able to move from contract signing to approval in eight weeks.

    “By deploying our platform to both patients and healthcare providers we can remove a lot of friction on both ends of the journey. With that in mind, we want to be where people are already going and help make that experience more meaningful.” remarked Coniglio.

    “Brands spend millions on patient support programs that patients don’t end up using in large part because they are unaware. We can be the glue that links these disparate silos together.”.
