    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause.
    • We are seeking a detail-oriented QA Specialist to ensure that every email and SMS campaign and journey is configured correctly and functions as intended prior to launch.
    • Conduct QA on all email and SMS campaigns and journeys in Iterable prior to launch to ensure every element is configured correctly and functions as intended.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause. We’ve built all of our technology in-house including an EHR, patient care admin system, patient portal, website, marketing technology etc. Winona has two compounding pharmacies and a team of in-house physicians providing world-class care via a fully vertically integrated business model.

    We are seeking a detail-oriented QA Specialist to ensure that every email and SMS campaign and journey is configured correctly and functions as intended prior to launch. This role spans campaign configuration and tracking, content and design review, and cross-platform QA — identifying and resolving problems before they reach our audience.

    Seniority Level: Junior–Mid Level.

    Conduct QA on all email and SMS campaigns and journeys in Iterable prior to launch to ensure every element is configured correctly and functions as intended.

    Verify campaign and journey names against Winona’s naming conventions (name, year, event, medium and audience).

    Review journey configuration, including start tiles, suppressions, scheduled send dates and times, tile logic and conditionals, entry limits, exit rules and journey event tracking.

    Confirm that monthly and recurring journeys are refreshed with updated start tiles prior to each send.

    Verify that campaign labels are applied correctly (audience, segments, category, goal and month/year).

    Confirm that the appropriate conversion events are assigned for each campaign type: prospect, customer upsell, Shop, community and live event campaigns.

    Review delivery settings, including quiet hours, send time optimization, frequency caps and performance alerts.

    Verify that link tracking is configured correctly, including Google Analytics, UTM parameters and custom link parameters.

    Review sender details: message type, from name, from email and reply-to address.

    Review email templates against Winona’s brand and design standards, including fonts, sizing, padding, CTA button styling, link formatting and footers.

    Test all links, CTA buttons and image links, and confirm that images include alt text.

    Proofread copy for accuracy, consistency and formatting.

    Send and review test proofs in light and dark mode on iOS and Android, across both Gmail and Apple Mail.

    Coordinate SMS test sends with the appropriate team members prior to testing.

    Conduct QA on email touchpoints that connect to Shopify, such as Shop campaigns and checkout-related flows, to ensure a seamless end-to-end experience.

    Follow and help maintain internal templating documentation, QA checklists and the HTML template library.

    Communicate concerns, errors and inconsistencies to the lifecycle team clearly and promptly, and track them through resolution.

    Recommend improvements to QA processes and standards on an ongoing basis.

    At least 3 years of experience performing QA within an ESP like Iterable or similar platforms.

    Working knowledge of HTML and CSS for email.

    Exceptional attention to detail and consistent checklist execution.

    Understanding of how emails render across clients, devices and dark mode.

    Clear written communication for reporting issues.

    Proficiency with Handlebars or dynamic content personalization.

    Shopify experience, particularly with checkout and order flows.

    Experience with email testing tools such as Litmus or Email on Acid.

    Familiarity with Google Analytics and UTM tracking.

    Experience with ClickUp or similar project management tools.

    Knowledge of SMS best practices and compliance standards (CAN-SPAM, CASL).

    As a full-time independent contractor, you’ll enjoy:.

    Remote-first, work wherever you choose.

    Paid non-working holidays per country of residence.

    Pro-rated 13th-month bonus in select regions.

    Financial support for online courses.

    Fun and casual work environment.

    Employee engagement activities and virtual gatherings.

    In a recent development, we are a diverse, global team! 🌍.

    #89412. OpenAI Getting Rid of Custom GPTs and Moving to Plugin Architecture

    📅 05 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (617 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    OpenAI Getting Rid of Custom GPTs and Moving to Plugin Architecture

    📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OpenAI has revealed it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a new plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.
    • Industry observers note that custom GPT retirement is currently scheduled for Dec.
    • For affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OpenAI has revealed it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a new plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.

    Industry observers note that custom GPT retirement is currently scheduled for Dec. 11, 2026, although the organization indicates timing and migration availability can vary by account and workspace.

    For affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct. 26 for ending creation of newly introduced Custom GPTs. Qualifying Enterprise customers with approved deferrals can continue using them until Feb. 11, 2027.

    OpenAI has changed its UI to make GPTs less prominent, and when customers choose to try creating a new Custom GPT, they are now prompted with an option to create a plugin instead.

    Rather than maintaining separate customized versions of ChatGPT, OpenAI is shifting customization toward plugins that can package reusable instructions, reference material, and connections to outside services.

    In a recent development, under OpenAI's plugin architecture, a plugin can include one or more skills containing instructions and resources for repeatable workflows, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing tools and external systems, or both. ChatGPT and Codex share a universal plugin directory, although some capabilities can remain specific to a particular environment.

    In a recent development, for organizations, that makes the change more than a simple renaming exercise. A organization could package recurring workflows into skills while using MCP servers or connected apps to give those workflows access to enterprise systems and data.

    OpenAI claims creators will be able to migrate an existing GPT through the My GPTs interface. The GPT's instructions become a skill in the replacement plugin, while knowledge files are copied into plugin reference files and connected apps can be carried over.

    In a recent development, not everything transfers automatically. Existing GPT conversations do not migrate, the selected model does not carry over, and Custom Actions may have to be rebuilt using an available app or a custom MCP server.

    Sharing also changes. Migrated plugins start private, existing GPT owners do not automatically receive access to the replacement, and prior sharing settings do not carry over.

    OpenAI is also cautioning organizations against assuming that migration will preserve behavior exactly. "A migrated plugin may respond differently," the company indicates, recommending that people retest familiar prompts, reference-material use, required output formats, and integrations before relying on the replacement.

    That warning has contributed to pushback from some GPT builders, who argue that plugins do not fully reproduce the dedicated and predictable environment of a Custom GPT. Other complaints have focused on sharing, migration complexity, and differences in how migrated workflows use instructions and reference material.

    Despite those concerns, OpenAI is clearly consolidating around plugins as its common mechanism for extending its AI products. Its developer documentation now describes plugins as packages owners can "discover, install, share, and publish" across ChatGPT and Codex, replacing the separate-custom-assistant model with reusable AI capabilities that can be combined with enterprise tools and services.

    For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

    David Ramel is an editor and writer at Converge 360.

    #89404. Industry News: AI Ambitions Are Running Into a Network Infrastructure Trust Problem

    📅 05 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (781 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: AI Ambitions Are Running Into a Network Infrastructure Trust Problem

    📅 05 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.
    • According to recent reports, the research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years.
    • The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.

    According to recent reports, the research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years. Among respondents whose initiatives were affected, AI and data-driven projects were the most cited, at 49%. That put AI ahead of security and compliance programs at 44%, digital transformation at 42%, and cloud migration at 38%.

    The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.

    All respondents worked for organizations with more than 2,000 employees and influenced network strategy across data centers, cloud, and connectivity. Of those surveyed, 66% had final sign-off responsibility. The results suggest that as organizations pursue increasingly data-intensive AI projects, confidence in the network infrastructure supporting them could become another deployment obstacle.

    Industry observers note that on the surface, Arelion found little evidence of a trust crisis. A total of 93% of respondents noted they largely or completely trust their current network provider, while 83% said that trust has strengthened over time.

    The picture changes when respondents are asked about a serious network incident. Only 15% remarked they have complete confidence in their provider's ability to quickly detect and address such a problem. Another 42% said their provider seriously lets them down anywhere from a few times a year to monthly or more frequently.

    Industry observers note that those concerns have consequences beyond the network itself. Responding organizations have delayed, scaled back, or stopped strategic initiatives because of provider trust concerns, while others have added resiliency or risk-mitigation measures.

    AI and data projects were the most affected among respondents reporting an impact, as organizations try to move AI from experimentation into larger production deployments.

    A serious provider failure could also have substantial consequences. Forty percent of respondents remarked such an event would cause major operational disruption, while 18% anticipated significant financial loss or severe financial or reputational damage.

    Sources indicate that another tension runs through Arelion's findings. Enterprises need networks they can trust to support AI projects, but many of the same decision-makers are concerned about AI's growing role inside those networks. A total of 54% of respondents identified AI and automation in network management and security as the factors most likely to negatively affect network trust over the next three years. That ranked ahead of data sovereignty expectations and geopolitical instability, both at 39%, and regulatory requirements and quantum computing threats to current encryption standards, both at 38%.

    At the same time, respondents aren't rejecting AI as a network technology. Proactive AI-driven fault prediction was among the capabilities they said would matter most to future trust, alongside stronger built-in security, greater accountability, and responsive support. That leaves enterprises in an unusual position: AI is increasing their dependence on digital infrastructure while also raising questions about how that infrastructure itself is managed.

    Recent findings suggest that arelion has an interest in emphasizing the importance of network-provider trust, and the survey reflects the views specifically of network decision-makers at large enterprises. Still, the findings point to an infrastructure consideration that can get lost amid the rush to adopt upcoming AI models and agents. AI projects ultimately depend on the networks, cloud environments, data centers, and connectivity beneath them. If organizations lack confidence in that foundation, access to better AI models alone won't remove the obstacle.

    Recent findings suggest that "Trust is influencing which strategic initiatives move forward, how organizations manage risk, and which providers they choose to work with," stated Mattias Fridström, Vice President at Arelion. "As businesses become increasingly reliant on digital infrastructure, enterprises are looking for network providers that can demonstrate transparency, accountability, and operational excellence, not just availability.".

    The full report is available for download here at the Arelion site (registration required).

    California Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing a latest model of artificial intelligence regulation that would give independent organizations a formal role in evaluating the safety claims made by AI giants.

    Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research from Digital Realty.
